A Border That No Law Can Fully Protect
September 21, 2026
6 min read

FAFACOUROU, Senegal – The day before, community members had swept every corner of the village school and arranged rows of chairs beneath a wide blue tarpaulin stretched taut against the September sun, the kind of preparation usually reserved for a wedding.

By the morning of September 16, everyone here knew something was happening. Women stirred enormous pots over open fires. Children darted between arriving guests, chasing each other around a banner that read, in English and French: Cross-border Meeting, The Gambia, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Together, let us act beyond borders to promote the abandonment of violence and harmful practices. Elders in flowing boubous exchanged greetings with young men and women wearing white caps stitched with the meeting’s logo.

Before a single official spoke, Fafacourou's young people acted out the violence they're determined to end.

Before a single mayor or governor had said a word, the community itself opened the day, acting out scenes of gender-based violence and harmful practices in the open space at the center of the courtyard, right in front of the officials who’d traveled here to discuss them.

Government and community leaders from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau spent the day working through a problem no single country can solve on its own. It was the communities themselves who organized the gathering, in partnership with Tostan and with support from UNFPA and the Italian Cooperation. They designed its program and opened the day in their own voice.

The reason is geography. Along this border, families share the same languages, the same customs, the same relatives on both sides.

When one country tightens its laws against female genital cutting or child marriage, some families simply cross into the next one. Senegal banned the practice in 1999. In 2024, Gambian lawmakers rejected a bill that would have repealed the country’s own ban, a reminder of how close the region came to losing ground on a practice already outlawed for nearly a decade.

“Our borders are very porous,” said Lawa Dramé, senior gender officer at the Gambian Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Welfare. “No country can do this alone.”

The data, drawn from national surveys and government ministries across the three countries, explain why this gathering matters. In Senegal, nearly 3 in 10 women have experienced some form of violence in the past year, according to the country’s first national survey on violence against women; roughly 1 in 5 women aged 15 to 49 have undergone genital cutting, a rate that climbs above 60 percent in the Kolda region itself. In Gambia, nearly 3 in 4 women aged 15 to 49 have undergone the practice, according to the 2019–2020 Demographic and Health Survey. In Guinea-Bissau, 52 percent of girls and women aged 15 to 49 have been subjected to the practice, according to UNICEF, and 26 percent of women aged 20 to 24 report having been married before the age of 18.

These are not distant statistics for the people gathered under that tarpaulin. They are neighbors, sisters and daughters.

Coumba Kandé was two years old when she was cut, too young to remember choosing anything, but not too young, she says, to remember the pain. She grew up in Fafacourou (Senegal’s Kolda region), cut years after Senegal had already outlawed the practice, a quiet illustration of how far a law can sit from what actually happens in a village. Now 22, unmarried and without children of her own, she sat among the delegations that day carrying something the speeches could only gesture toward: what it means to live inside a statistic.

That day, she stood before elders and officials and spoke without hesitation, her voice carrying one demand: that no girl after her must feel unprotected.

In an interview afterward, she explained what stood behind those words. “I was cut when I was two,” she said. “But I still remember how it all went. I have never felt that much pain in my whole life. If I had been given the choice, I would not have gone through it.”

Through community awareness programs, she later learned about the practice’s long-term health consequences, a discovery that left her, in her own words, unsettled about what her body might still face.

Cut at two, Coumba Kandé, 22, stood before elders and demanded that no girl after her feel unprotected.

“I am not married yet and I don’t have children,” she said, “but I feel vulnerable.”

Fafacourou’s agenda reached beyond cutting alone. Early and forced marriage, Africa’s other most pressing harmful practice, carries a cost that extends beyond any single girl’s life. A World Bank report found that child marriage costs twelve African countries, representing half the continent’s population, an estimated $63 billion in lost earnings and productivity, driven largely by its effect on girls’ education and on fertility and population growth. The economic case and the human rights case point in the same direction.

Mayors, governors, and préfets from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau arrived to discuss a border no single law protects.

Governor Ousman Bah of The Gambia’s Central River Region, who traveled to Fafacourou for the meeting, put it plainly. “These communities share the same borders, cultures, families, and social connections,” he said. “We cannot address challenges affecting these communities by working in isolation.”

Watching that day, he said that he recognized exactly what ECOWAS envisions under its Pillar 5, proof, in his words, that the region’s development goals and a village courtyard in Kolda point in the same direction.

Then he reached for a metaphor closer to home. “I often think of life as a bucket that is passed from one generation to another,” he said. “Our parents passed that bucket to us. We have a responsibility to protect it, preserve it, and pass it safely to our children.”

Community leaders on the ground already understand the logic instinctively. A girl protected in one village is not fully protected if the girl in the next village, across an invisible line, is not. Ending these practices will take the same coordination across borders that families already use to escape the law.

No single meeting closes that gap. But for one day in Fafacourou, three countries chose to try to close it together.

Abandoning Female Genital Cutting: ‘It wasn’t the fear of prison that changed things’
August 7, 2026
4 min read

THIARAP, Senegal — Under a makeshift shelter that offers little relief from the heat of this June morning, Samba Baldé turns a string of prayer beads slowly between his fingers. Around him, village elders fan themselves against the humid air settling over Thiarap, a small rural community in Fouladou, southern Senegal. In a matter of days, this village and 26 others across the Coumbacara district will gather for a big event: a public declaration ending female genital cutting and child marriage in their communities. At 65, the village chief remembers a time when the practice was simply considered part of a girl’s life.

For us, it was custom. We didn’t think we were doing something wrong, He says.

The subject remains especially sensitive in the Kolda region, where FGC prevalence reaches as high as 63.6 percent, among the highest in Senegal, according to UNICEF. Senegal outlawed the practice in 1999, with penalties of up to five years in prison for anyone who performs or orders it. Yet the practice persisted because adherence to community tradition mattered more in daily life than compliance with the law.

A few years after the law passed, that gap produced a moment Thiarap still remembers. Police came from Kolda, the regional capital, and gathered the village’s elders (men and women together) into a truck bound for the city, to be questioned over a cutting ceremony that had just taken place. After the investigation, seven people were found responsible, among them the village chief himself, and were sentenced to four months and ten days in prison.

Yahya Diao, in his late sixties now too, was brought in with the others for questioning but was not among the seven sentenced. He describes what he saw during the hearings.

Yaya Diao was brought in for questioning after Thiarap's 1999 cutting case — he was not sentenced, but he remembers every detail of it

They put us all in a truck, the elders together,” he says. “We went to the hospital, the cutters too. The doctors examined the girls and confirmed it had happened.

The punishment shocked the village without changing much about how it lived.

We were punished, but we didn’t really understand why,” Baldé recalls. “We were told it was forbidden, but no one took the time to explain the consequences of the practice.

Nobody in Thiarap decided to defy the law outright. In villages like this one, far from the roads authorities travel and the offices where the law is enforced, families who wanted to continue the practice simply did, away from view, and a jail sentence handed down in one village doesn’t necessarily reach the next one over. FGC didn’t disappear from Fouladou so much as retreat from sight, a pattern Tostan has documented elsewhere in Senegal, in villages where isolation, not defiance, kept the law from ever really arriving.

Usually, when information comes from higher up, only people in the cities are told,” Diao says. “No one came to explain it to us.

Village chief Samba Baldé in Coumbacara during the June 14 declaration ending female genital cutting and child marriage

The turn came in 2024, when Thiarap joined Tostan’s Community Empowerment Program. Sessions were held in the language people spoke at home, led by people from their own community. Residents examined human rights, health, education, and the consequences of violence against women and girls together, with women, men, young people, religious leaders, and traditional authorities in the same room.

Baldé says no one forced their hand or threatened them a second time. What changed, he says, was that for the first time since the arrests, someone actually sat with them and laid out why the practice caused harm, and it was only then that the damage became clear to him; damage he hadn’t recognized before, and he began to regret it.

We didn’t abandon the practice because we were afraid,” he says. “We abandoned it because we understood.

On June 14, 2026, Thiarap participated alongside more than 500 participants from 27 communities in Coumbacara district for a public declaration against FGC and child marriage.

You can send everyone to jail,” Diao says, “but without understanding, people will still hold on to what they know. Because they believe they are right. Because no one explained anything to them, and no one discussed it with them. Then one day, someone comes and tells them to stop a practice their grandfathers and grandmothers did for centuries.

“Listen carefully…and support the people to build upon what they already know, value, and envision for their future.”

– Cheikh Anta DIOP
Tostan’s origins date back to 1974, when our founder, Molly Melching, first arrived in Senegal as an exchange student from the United States.

She initially came as a graduate student to study African literature written in French, but quickly realized that her true passion lay in development and in the study of national languages.

During this period, Molly was mentored by the renowned historian and scientist Dr. Cheikh Anta Diop. His vision of African self-determination and cultural pride deeply shaped her thinking. From him, she learned the importance of listening carefully, valuing what people already know, and building upon local knowledge and strengths—principles that later became the foundation of Tostan’s approach.

After completing her studies, Molly founded a children’s center in Dakar — where she worked for six years — that adapted children’s stories into Wolof, eventually developing an extensive library of children’s books in national languages. She also created the first radio program for children in national languages. Her work took her to rural villages, where she found that this lack of access to contextually relevant material did not just apply to literature; she saw how many development efforts were not addressing the true needs and realities of communities in ways that were relevant to their lives. Relying heavily on community feedback, Molly and a team of Senegalese cultural specialists developed a new type of development program,the Community Empowerment Program (CEP). This program respectfully engaged communities by working in their own languages and using traditional methods of learning. It facilitated community ownership over the development process, allowing communities to fulfill their own potential.

Their efforts grew throughout the 1980s, leading Molly to found Tostan which means breakthrough in the Wolof language in 1991. For over 30 years, Molly’s original concepts have developed into a leading model for community-led change; a model that has now been implemented in 22 languages across eight African countries, is shared internationally with activists and practitioners through our training seminars, and is supported at the international, national, and grassroots levels.

What Is at Stake

In rural areas of West Africa and the Sahel, communities face rising threats to peace and security. Violence-driven instability in countries such as Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger continues to grow, with insurgent, inter-communal and resource-related conflicts spreading across rural territories.

Conflicts between herders and farmers over land, water and grazing rights now claim thousands of lives across the region.
These dynamics disrupt livelihoods, hinder access to education and health services, displace families and erode community cohesion. Without effective local mechanisms for dialogue, mediation and collective decision-making, rural households – especially women, youth and marginalised groups – remain vulnerable to violence, exclusion and cycles of retaliation.
Given this context, strengthening grassroots resilience, local leadership and inclusive peacebuilding is essential for sustainable development, wellbeing and stability.

What We Are Doing

The Peace and Security module gives communities practical tools to prevent conflict and strengthen local mediation. Trained facilitators lead 21 sessions in local languages with men, women, and youth. Participants review their community vision, discuss rights and responsibilities, and learn how dialogue supports peace and human security. Each community creates a Peace Commission within the Community Management Committee (CMCs). These groups monitor tensions, mediate disputes, and implement action plans that promote safety and cooperation. After completing the sessions, participants reach out to neighbouring villages to share what they learned and encourage a wider culture of peace.

What Change Looks Like

Communities report fewer confrontations and greater trust between groups. Peace Commissions meet regularly to prevent small disputes from escalating. Women and youth take on active roles in mediation and local decision making. Youth participate in outreach and help connect communities that once viewed each other with suspicion. Local dialogues replace rumours and conflict, and communities work together to resolve issues related to land, water, or daily life. These changes create safer environments where families can focus on education, livelihoods, and community priorities without fear of violence.

With strengthened relationships, communities drive lasting shifts in norms, peace, and equity, and reinforce new, more inclusive governance practices.

In many of the communities where Tostan works, traditional roles, exclusion, and cycles of violence limit what people believe is possible. Practices such as female genital cutting (FGC), child marriage, and gender-based violence are upheld by social norms, perpetuate inequality, and hinder development.

The process of social transformation begins early in the Community Empowerment Program. In the Kobi phase, participants collectively define their common vision of wellbeing. They explore principles of human rights, the related responsibilities, and shared values. They reflect on how these principles apply in daily life. They explore how their practices align with these principles and begin to question practices that cause harm. Using dialogue, storytelling, and cultural learning tools, communities begin to envision alternative futures.

As learning deepens, communities learn how to engage in peaceful communication, conflict resolution, mediation, and collective decision making. Open dialogue, sharing, and learning about rights and communication enable them to reduce violence and strengthen relationships between groups such as men and women or youth and elders. These stronger connections make it possible to engage in open, respectful dialogues about sensitive issues and to agree on new directions. 

Change spreads further through Tostan’s organized diffusion strategy, in which participants share what they learn with relatives and with neighboring villages. The dialogues often culminate in public declarations where villages and their kin networks commit to work together toward attaining the principles of human dignity, including by abandoning harmful practices.

Over time, networks of communities, together with religious leaders and local authorities, reinforce new practices until they become the new social norm.

Respect and peace are enhanced and violence decreases within households as well as throughout the communities.

Early Child Development
Parents and caregivers gain practical tools to support children’s early learning
What Is at Stake

Young children in rural areas often grow up with limited early learning opportunities. Studies show that more than 60 percent of children in Sub Saharan Africa are at risk of not reaching their developmental potential due to low stimulation and limited access to early learning resources. Research  in West Africa  also finds that children in rural households experience fewer activities that support language and cognitive growth, such as storytelling, naming objects, or being asked questions.

Long distances to preschools, limited parental support materials, and unequal access to health and nutrition services deepen the challenge. Caregivers who did not attend school often believe they cannot support their child’s learning. Women and youth carry most caregiving responsibilities yet receive little training or guidance.

When these gaps persist, children start school with lower readiness, which affects long term learning, confidence, and wellbeing.

What We Are Doing

The Reinforcement of Parental Practices module strengthens early childhood development by giving parents and caregivers practical tools to support their children’s growth from birth.

Our approach builds on the Community Empowerment Program (CEP) and focuses on simple daily practices that stimulate the brain. Parents learn how to talk to children using richer vocabulary, ask questions, tell stories, copy playful behavior, and describe objects in detail. Facilitators lead these sessions in local languages and link early childhood care to children’s rights, dignity, and wellbeing.

The module also supports collective reflection on social norms that influence parenting. Religious leaders, elders, youth, and caregivers take part in discussions on how to adapt daily practices in ways that reflect new knowledge.

To increase access, communities use Vroom Tips and the Amplio Talking Book, an audio tool for caregivers with limited literacy. These tools help families apply new practices in daily routines.

HOW DOES TOSTAN’S EDUCATION PROGRAM FOSTER SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION ?
FIND OUT MORE
What Change Looks Like

Communities report clear improvements in early childhood care.

Parents now speak more with their children and feel confident in their role as first educators. Women and youth caregivers use books and audio tools during daily routines. Storytelling traditions have returned, and elders participate more actively in early learning activities.

Families report less corporal punishment and better school readiness. Children show stronger language, social, and emotional skills. They enter school more prepared to learn and engage.

These changes support lifelong learning, strengthen family relationships, and contribute to a community environment where every child has the chance to grow, thrive, and participate fully in future opportunities.

Economic Development
Participants in Tostan’s education program develop the skills needed to manage projects and run small businesses.
What’s at Stake

Although many African economies have experienced rapid growth over the past few years, unemployment remains high and economic opportunities in rural areas are still limited, especially for women.
When a family is struggling economically, girls are more likely than boys to be taken out of school to help with income-generating activities or agricultural labor, and they are more likely to be married at a young age.

We believe that communities can manage their own economic development in ways that make sense for their family and their communities.

What We’re Doing

The final phase of the CEP, the Aawde, includes class sessions on basic literacy, math, project management, and budgeting skills that help participants successfully plan and launch small businesses in their communities.

We also provide small Community Development Grants to Community Management Committees (CMC). The CMCs often use these grants to establish a rotating microcredit fund that helps community members, particularly women, with the investment they need to start small businesses, invest in agriculture, or take on other income-generating activities. The CMC also encourages community members to save and plan for the future.

HOW DOES TOSTAN’S EDUCATION PROGRAM FOSTER SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION ?
FIND OUT MORE
Microgrants in Covid-19

During the unprecedented events caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, Tostan partnered with the Mastercard Foundation from 2020-2022 to support the most vulnerable households in Senegal – in the departments of Médina Yoro Foula, the regions of Kolda and Ranérou, and the region of Matam. Tostan and the Mastercard Foundation piloted an unconditional micro-grant initiative that was launched and monitored with the help of local authorities and Community Management Committees. Over 2,000 households (mostly women as recipients) were beneficiaries of approximately $115 each spread over three instalments. According to the reported findings by IDInsight, the majority of beneficiaries found the grant useful, spending most of their money on food, followed by productive purchases, education and health care.

What Change Looks Like

Community Management Committees have successfully used grants of $300-$1,000 to launch small businesses including selling basic food staples; making and selling products like soap, mosquito-repellent lotion, fruit juices, or dyed fabric; and organizing collective projects such as community gardens and animal-raising cooperatives. Many of these small businesses are run by women, offering them the opportunity to earn an independent income.

Through the Empowered Communities Network, we connect communities with local and international organizations to work together on small business ventures and microcredit programs.

Education
Adults and youth in our education program gain skills to address key issues and strengthen learning in their families and communities.
What’s at Stake

For adults and youth who have not had access to formal school or who left school early, few or no educational resources exist to help them understand and navigate the challenges they face. 

For those where formal school is an option, school facilities are often inadequate and located at great distances from communities. Many families still prioritize sending boys to school, keeping girls at home to help with housework, agriculture, and looking after other siblings.

UNICEF and others have shown that educating girls not only helps them to become financially independent in the future, but also leads to decreases in maternal and infant mortality. Educated mothers are more likely to share good health practices with their families and communities, and they are more likely to send their own daughters to school.

What We’re Doing

Tostan’s program provides a comprehensive non-formal education solution that supports adults and adolescents with a range of knowledge, skills and experiences that help them navigate many important areas.

The entire program is designed to provide a foundational, empowering education for those who have previously had little or no formal education. This supports them to identify and work towards improved well-being – including education for their families.

The curriculum also provides vital educational resources. In particular, in the final phase of Tostan’s Community Empowerment Program (CEP) , the Aawde, participants learn basic literacy skills in their local languages, as well as basic math skills. They learn how to send and receive SMS text messages, through our Mobile Phone for Literacy and Development module, which also encourages participants to practice and share their newly acquired literacy skills. Similarly, through our Reinforcement of Parental Practices Module, communities learn new ways to support their children at home in preparation for school.

Tostan also trains community leaders to organize for community well-being in education, and to advocate with local education partners for better services and resources.

HOW DOES TOSTAN’S EDUCATION PROGRAM FOSTER SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION ?
FIND OUT MORE
What Change Looks Like

Communities transform the knowledge they learn during the Community Empowerment Program (CEP) into action, creating access to education for all.

Our CEP has increased primary school enrollment and retention rates and provided adult participants with basic literacy skills.

Community Management Committees (CMC) lead initiatives that ensure girls and boys are enrolled in school. When a family is considering removing their child from school, CMC members meet with them to discuss other possible solutions. If there are no public schools in the area, they petition the local government to build one.

Many communities have shown increased school enrolment for girls in the years following their participation in the program. As participating communities – and their neighbors – often pledge to abandon child marriage, girls are likely to stay in school for longer.

Tostan’s education program supports communities to lead initiatives that promote sustainable solutions to environmental issues and strengthen climate resilience.
What’s at Stake

The climate crisis adds pressure to an already fragile situation in many rural areas. Communities across West Africa and the Sahel face unpredictable rainfall, land degradation, poor water and waste management, soil erosion, growing desertification, and higher disease risks.

Many partner communities lack adequate sanitation, which increases health problems. Climate shocks also threaten agriculture and raise the risk of food insecurity. Recent assessments show that many families now eat only one meal per day.

Women, youth and other marginalized groups face the greatest impact. Women make up about 70 percent of the agricultural workforce, yet they often have limited access to land, extension services, and quality

What We’re Doing

Our Community Empowerment Program (CEP) equips community members with the knowledge and skills to find creative and sustainable solutions to problems. During the CEP, participants learn how the most common diseases are transmitted. They also learn about the ways in which environmental conditions contribute to health challenges and measures they can take to address them. Our respectful and non-judgmental approach promotes community discussion about the environment. As a result, communities lead initiatives to make their environments more resilient in order to protect the community’s wider health.

The CEP also supports communities to install and use basic, available technologies such as adapted wood stoves and to conduct collective projects like tree-planting. We partner with environmental organizations such as Seed Program International and Taaru Askan to offer equitable access to agricultural skills training and resources for women such as quality seed. The aim is to enable community members to implement decentralized, small-scale food production and income-generation strategies that are resilient to climate change and enrich rather than degrade the land.

Finally, Tostan’s model supports the resilience of communities and women and girls more broadly through our training in leadership, financial management, and literacy to help them find new economic opportunities and build their capacity to identify and make progress on a range of areas, increasing their resilience in the face of the climate crisis and other interconnected challenges.

What Change Looks Like

Many communities now hold weekly clean-ups, joining together to pick up garbage, clear grass, and rid their environment of standing water to create a clean and healthy living space. They also construct latrines to prevent the spread of illness and parasites, build more efficient wood-burning stoves which reduce wood gathering time and overall wood consumption, and construct covers for wells to protect the water from contaminants.

Health
Tostan’s education program supports partner communities to understand health risks and make health, hygiene, and disease prevention a priority.
What’s at Stake

 The health of children and adults is at risk in communities because of limited access to health resources and basic health care, low vaccination rates, and limited awareness about disease prevention and hygiene practices such as hand washing to prevent the spread of germs and illness. What’s more, women and girls can face particular challenge in accessing basic health services such as pre- and post-natal consultations.

In many of the communities where Tostan works, child marriage and female genital cutting (FGC) are common practices. A girl who is not cut can be ostracized from her community and may not be able to marry. However, there is a lack of awareness of the negative impact on girls’ and women’s physical and emotional health, including significantly higher risks during pregnancy and childbirth.

What We’re Doing

During our Community Empowerment Program, participants learn about their right to health and their right to be free from all forms of violence, about hygiene, and how common diseases such as diarrhea and malaria are spread and prevented. Very often the program is the first opportunity they have had to learn about these topics in local languages. They also discuss the health risks of harmful practices such as FGC and child marriage.

Our program encourages community members to share the knowledge they gain about health and human rights with their social networks, and helps communities to coordinate with local actors in the health system. 

The program also helps communities connect with one another to discuss vital health topics and potential solutions.

HOW DOES TOSTAN’S EDUCATION PROGRAM FOSTER SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION ?
FIND OUT MORE
What Change Looks Like

Communities often launch specific initiatives to improve child and maternal health in their villages. They raise awareness on the importance of vaccinations as well as take action to improve community hygiene and prevent diseases such as malaria. They also construct local health huts and coordinate with local government resources on vaccination campaigns, and they encourage pre- and post-natal visits, and other essential health practices. 

They also lead major efforts to end harmful practices. Between 1991 and 2021, 5,700,000 people living in 9,517 communities across eight African countries have publicly declared their intention to end FGC and child marriage following their direct or indirect engagement in our Community Empowerment Program.

As awareness has grown and a critical mass has been building, thousands of villages have joined the movement for the abandonment of FGC in Senegal. We hope to see a national-level public declaration within the next few years.

Community-led efforts in the area of maternal and child health have led to a rise in vaccination rates, an increase in attendance at prenatal and postnatal consultations, and a decline in children suffering from malnutrition.

With good governance and social transformation communities take individual and collective actions that result in human development outcomes

Limited resources and education, poor health, malnutrition, and environmental pressures affect millions across rural communities in West Africa.

The Community Empowerment Program (CEP) integrates literacy, health, education, nutrition, economic opportunity, and environmental stewardship into one holistic journey. In the Kobi phase, participants collectively reflect on the principles of human rights and democracy and develop skills in problem solving. They then learn about health, hygiene, and disease prevention and apply the learning in line with the principles they agreed on. In the Aawde phase, they build literacy, numeracy, financial planning, and project management skills, enabling them to act on their priorities.

As they learn, communities put new knowledge into practice, with the support and leadership of their Community Management Committee (CMC). They organize vaccination and maternal health campaigns, support birth registration, engage in parent-teacher associations in schools, and introduce improved sanitation facilities. They strengthen economic wellbeing as CMCs support small projects and income-generating activities. 

Environmental sessions encourage communities to reflect on land, water, and climate, and take steps to protect their ecosystems. These efforts are reinforced by CMCs’ collaboration with local authorities, ensuring sustainable systems of support.

COVID-19 Resources Co-created With Communities

At the start of the pandemic, Tostan worked with partner communities and health experts to produce clear information in local languages. These tools helped thousands of families understand the virus and protect themselves. They remain available for anyone supporting community learning today. 

Tostan created two open-source booklets to provide rural communities with accurate information on COVID-19. The materials were developed with health specialists and local leaders to reflect daily realities, social norms, and trusted sources of guidance.

This booklet explains how COVID-19 spreads, key symptoms to watch for, and simple prevention steps adapted to village life. It includes official contact numbers for reliable information and support.

Religious Perspective on Epidemics, Pandemics, and Contagious Diseases

Written by Imam Mamadou Chérif Diop, this resource brings together relevant Qur’anic verses and faith-based guidance. It reinforces public health advice and helps communities understand the pandemic through a religious lens. 

How these tools supported communities during the pandemic

By December 2020, Tostan printed and shared more than 70,000 copies across hundreds of partner communities in the Gambia, Guinea, Guinea Bissau, Mali, and Senegal. Local radio stations helped broadcast the content. Government partners distributed the materials to health and education centers, which strengthened local prevention efforts and supported community-led action.

Languages available

The booklets are available in 15 languages: Bamanankan, Creole, English, French, Fula (Pulaar), Haussa, Igbo, Mandinka, Maninka, Oniyan, Portuguese, Somali, Swahili, Wolof, and Yoruba.

Permissions

You may reprint the booklets for educational or non-commercial use if the content remains unchanged. Any adaptation requires written permission from Tostan. For reproduction requests or printer-ready files, contact info@tostan.org.

These resources reflect Tostan’s long experience in community education and social norms change. They provided timely, life-saving information during COVID-19 and continue to support organizations working with rural communities today.

Ending Child Marriage and Cutting : The Generation Born After
October 22, 2026
4 min read

Marième Bamba was 13 when she was married, with no say in the decision. At 13, her daughter Adama was in school.

The years between those two facts hold a question that has followed West Africa’s movement against female genital cutting and child marriage from its start.

Communities can decide to abandon a practice. Does that decision hold for daughters too young to have taken part in it, and for their daughters after them?

The answer matters well beyond one village. In Senegal, three in ten women aged 20 to 24 were married before 18, and nearly one in ten before 15, according to the 2023 Demographic and Health Survey. Cutting follows ethnic lines more closely than regional ones. Fatick, a largely Serer region, records some of the lowest rates in the country. Soudiane is a Bambara village, and there, Marième recalls, nearly every girl of her generation was cut.

Adama was born in Soudiane in 1998. Girls there were usually cut in early childhood, often by the age of four or five. Adama never was. That same year when she was born, the village had declared publicly that it would abandon both cutting and child marriage.

She lost nothing by abandoning those practices,- Adama says of her mother.

Her mother had taken part in the discussions that led to it. In 1999, the year Senegal made cutting a criminal offense, Marième joined the community-led education program Tostan facilitated in Soudiane in Bamanankan.

The sessions began with human rights and shared responsibilities, and asked participants to find them in their own culture and religion.

Then came the harder question of which of their practices failed to respect them. Cutting usually surfaced through the right to be free from violence.

Women who had each carried its pain alone began to describe it aloud, and found the ordeal was common to them all. Marième carried her share.

Her first pregnancy, soon after her marriage, came with complications she attributes to the cutting. The law set the rule, and deliberation shifted the norm the law depended on.

 Adama grew up watching what else shifted. Her mother learned to read and write to manage the village’s projects, and became coordinator of its Community Management Committee. Her commitment won her six months of training as a solar engineer at Barefoot College in India. The trip also needed her husband’s agreement to six months apart, a measure of how far expectations of women in Soudiane had moved. Marième came home and wired 50 households, work that in the village had belonged to men. Adama says it showed her that what a man can do, a woman can do too. As a community birth attendant, her mother refused to turn away women who could not pay, sometimes covering the cost herself. Adama says that is part of why she became a nurse. Marième’s path, told elsewhere, earned her the Pioneer Woman Award in 2022. 

Adama now has a daughter of her own, two years old. She has said many times that the girl will not be cut. Nor does she treat her mother’s choices as a ceiling.

As young people, we should do more than what she’s achieved,- she says.

By more, she means carrying her mother’s work forward, with knowledge Marième gained only as an adult and Adama’s generation has had from the start.
One family is not a trend. Adama grew up with a mother who became a public figure, a model few girls in rural Senegal have. This story cannot tell us whether the decision holds in households where mothers took no leadership role, or among daughters who moved to cities, where a village agreement carries less weight.

Before her daughter was born, Adama spoke to her the way her mother once spoke to her,

just like two adults.

The girl is two now, nearing the age at which Soudiane once cut her daughters. For Adama, that question was answered a generation ago.

Tostan is recruiting a Regional Partnerships Manager to join its Partnerships Department. The position is based in Thiès, Senegal.

Your role

Reporting to the Chief Partnerships Officer, you will lead the development, cultivation and growth of Tostan’s regional and institutional partnerships portfolio. You will turn Tostan’s strategic priorities into a focused portfolio of high-potential accounts and opportunities, and move them from early positioning through qualification, conversion, negotiation, renewal and growth. You will also serve as a source of institutional partnership expertise across Tostan, and supervise the Partnerships Development Officer.

Key responsibilities

Partnerships development, engagement and positioning (40%)

Lead engagement with priority regional and institutional partners: governments and public institutions, United Nations agencies, multilateral and bilateral donors, African regional and sub-regional institutions, development banks and development finance actors, institutional foundations, and selected private-sector partners.
Develop tailored engagement strategies for priority accounts and build relationships with decision-makers and influential stakeholders.
Position Tostan early in relevant funding and partnership discussions, including before formal opportunities are launched.
Represent Tostan in selected donor consultations, strategic forums, regional platforms and partnership spaces.
Identify and develop strategic partnerships and consortia where Tostan has a clear comparative role.
Work with the CEO, CPO and other senior leaders to prepare and support high-level donor and partner engagement.

Portfolio development, resource mobilization and conversion (45%)

Manage a focused portfolio of priority accounts with clear strategies, relationship objectives and next actions.
Lead opportunity qualification and recommend whether to pursue, nurture, monitor or decline.
Serve as Opportunity Lead for selected high-value opportunities, mobilizing the appropriate deal team through cultivation, proposal development, negotiation and decision-making.
Work with Proposal/Program Liaison, Programs, MERL, Research, Finance and other teams to secure the technical, financial and evidence inputs required.
Provide strategic review and donor-positioning input for priority proposals and donor-facing materials.
Lead or support negotiations, and develop renewal, extension and account-growth strategies for existing partnerships.
Monitor portfolio performance against pipeline, conversion and revenue targets, and contribute to diversifying Tostan’s funding base.
Provide institutional partnership expertise for opportunities opened by country offices, affiliates, senior leadership or other teams.

Team leadership, coordination and organizational alignment (15%)

Supervise the Partnerships Development Officer, including priority setting, coaching, performance management and professional development.
Work closely with Global Philanthropy and National Partnerships to align partnership approaches.
Contribute to portfolio reviews, annual planning and departmental performance monitoring.
Support consistent use of the shared partnerships operating system: account ownership, opportunity roles, handoffs and qualification processes.
Escalate strategic decisions, major negotiations, portfolio conflicts or high-risk opportunities to the CPO as appropriate.

Profile

A master’s degree in a relevant field is welcomed and preferred.
Strong experience in institutional partnerships, resource mobilization, business development or strategic partnerships.
Demonstrated ability to develop and manage institutional donor or partner relationships.
Experience developing opportunities with governments, multilateral or bilateral organizations, foundations, regional institutions or related actors, from early engagement through proposal, negotiation and partnership development.
Strong understanding of institutional donor priorities, funding processes and partnership models.
Ability to manage a portfolio and prioritize among multiple accounts and opportunities.
Experience coordinating cross-functional teams around complex opportunities.
Fluency in French and English, written and spoken. Knowledge of a language spoken in Tostan countries is an asset.
Strategic in outlook and pragmatic in execution, with a collaborative leadership style.
Enjoys working in a small, mission-driven NGO and is comfortable across cultures, geographies and functions.
Commitment to Tostan’s mission and values.

2026 A season for sport.
A global youth event.

From 31 October to 13 November 2026, Senegal will host the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event held in Africa. The competitions will take place in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, all three urban areas. Yet nearly half of Senegalese live in rural areas. Millions of young people will watch this historic moment from far away, with no part in it. Many of them, especially girls, have few places to play organized sport and even fewer spaces where their views shape community decisions. Jo’tali starts there.

“While the world watches Dakar’s stadiums, I see girls across Senegal running a different race, towards freedom, confidence and choices of their own. The Games can inspire them. Their communities can help pave the way.”
Sobel A. Ngom
CEO, Tostan
WHY THIS MOMENT MATTERS
A Nation of Youth meets an Olympic first.

While 50% of Senegal’s population is under 19 years of age, many young people especially girls do not have the access or opportunities to participate in sports or experience the Games. Yet their perspectives matter to the future of their communities and their country.

JO’TALI helps this national moment become a community experience.

New study backs Tostan civic model
October 2, 2026
6 min read

Can you learn to govern outside a classroom?

A review of the research published this year argues that learning outside school can prepare Africans for public life. In three West African countries, women who left school or never went have shown what that looks like.

Fatimata Madina Baldé, Pirada, Guinea-Bissau. Married young, she now trains facilitators and leads radio discussions on early marriage.

THIÈS, Senegal — In Pirada, Guinea-Bissau, Fatimata Madina Baldé’s schooling ended when her family arranged her marriage. Her way back to learning was a class taught in Pular, her own language, by Tostan’s Community Empowerment Program (CEP). Today she trains facilitators and leads radio discussions on early marriage.

She left school but did not stop learning. Can learning like hers prepare people for public life, in places where school has not? A paper published this year asks exactly that.

The question matters most for the young. Africa’s median age is about 19, the lowest of any region, and the continent is governed by some of the world’s oldest leaders.

Young Africans are also the most schooled generation the continent has produced. Sixty-four percent have at least some secondary education, compared with 35 percent of people 56 and older, according to Afrobarometer. Yet they are less likely than their elders to vote, attend a community meeting or contact a local leader.

Something between the classroom and the ballot box is missing.

In the Journal of Academics Stand Against Poverty, the researcher Grace Gondwe argues that non-formal education, meaning structured learning outside the school system, can supply part of it. Her paper does not report new fieldwork. It reviews existing studies and evaluations, and it examines two programs closely.

The first is Solar Mamas in Zanzibar. There, women with little or no schooling spend six months training as solar engineers with India’s Barefoot College. The skill turns into standing: a woman who brings electricity to her village gets a voice when the village decides things.

The second is Tostan’s program, which works on a whole community at once. Participants, Gondwe writes, learn to negotiate, settle disputes and reach decisions together across lines of gender, age and status.

Gondwe treats these as two different routes to civic life. In Soudiane, a village in central Senegal, one woman took both. Marieme Bamba, who never went to school, was elected in 1999 to coordinate the management committee her village formed through Tostan’s program. Later she trained at Barefoot College and came home to bring solar light to 150 households.


Marieme Bamba, Soudiane, Senegal. Never schooled, she led her village committee and brought solar light to 150 homes.

In The Gambia, the results of this kind of learning were put to a vote.

In 2017, the government’s Women’s Bureau held grassroots elections to choose one woman from each district for the National Women’s Council, which advises on policies affecting women and girls. Each district covers 40 to 50 villages. In all seven districts of the Upper River Region, according to Tostan, voters chose a woman who had been through its program. Many had led their village’s management committee. Several said that before the classes, they had rarely spoken in public.

The government has taken note. Speaking at a Tostan seminar in 2021, Kajali Sonko, deputy permanent secretary at the Ministry of Women and Children’s Affairs, said the program had “greatly enhanced communities especially women and girls” in the Upper River Region in human rights, governance, health and education. That finding, he said, was confirmed by the Women’s Bureau’s own quarterly field monitoring.

Stories like these are not proof. The strongest numbers come from Senegal, and they are two decades old. In 2006, the political scientist Michelle Kuenzi published a survey of 1,484 rural Senegalese. She found that people who had gone through non-formal education in their own languages took part in political and community life at least as much as people who had been to school, and generally more.

That finding has limits. A 2023 study in Political Science Research and Methods found that in Senegal, education increased political participation only when democracy appeared to be under threat. Learning may prepare people to act. Circumstances seem to decide when they do.

Gondwe is also direct about Tostan’s room of improvement. The model depends on well-trained facilitators and on communities staying involved for years. She writes that attempts to expand it too quickly have already cost it quality and consistency, and that growth at that pace risks reducing a real process to a symbolic one. For that claim, she cites a 2017 report on social norms.

Tostan accepts part of the point.

This statement is partially true,

said Yussuf Sané, coordinator of Tostan’s Program Leadership Team.

Expansion without standardization and harmonization is a recipe for failure.

Tostan has since written a manual of procedures for its national teams to follow as they expand, he said, and supervisors accompany each facilitator at least three times a month. Facilitators still speak the community’s language and live there for the full three years.

Growth itself has changed, too. Instead of only

Replicating the full CEP in more communities,

said Aïssé Kane, Tostan’s Sharing and Mutual Learning Officer, the organization increasingly teaches its methods to local organizations that adapt them to their own contexts, as in its recent work in Benin and Ethiopia.

Gondwe’s larger argument concerns Africa’s place in the world. The African Union became a permanent member of the G20 in 2023. What the continent does with that seat, she argues, will depend less on how young its people are than on whether they are ready to lead. The African Union’s long-term plan, Agenda 2063, describes the Africa it wants as one whose development is “people-driven,” relying especially on its women and youth.

The plan does not say where those people will learn to lead.

Fatoumatta Jabbie, The Gambia. Once too shy to speak in public, she became vice-chair of the National Women's Council.

Before she trained as a Tostan facilitator, Fatoumatta Jabbie said, she was “shy and ashamed to speak in public.” In 2017 she campaigned across her district in the Upper River Region and won a seat on the National Women’s Council. She later became its vice-chair.

“I promised women of my area that they will have a stronger voice at the council when I am elected,” she said, “and that is exactly what I am doing.”

Education and family support for successful reintegration

The Prison Project supports detainees to reintegrate into their communities through a tailored version of Tostan’s Community Empowerment Program (CEP). Participants learn about human rights and acquire practical skills to start income-generating activities. The program also facilitates family mediations to help former detainees rebuild relationships and reintegrate smoothly after release.

The Prison Project is currently active in nine men’s and women’s prisons across Senegal.

What's at Stake

In countries where we work, state prisons often lack water, toilets, adequate space for living and recreation, and medical services. They also usually lack organized rehabilitation activities for prisoners. Without education or reintegration support, the risk of reoffending remains high.

The Prison Project responds to this challenge by providing access to education, dialogue, and personal development within prison settings. It operates under international frameworks that encourage partnerships between correctional institutions and organizations like Tostan to promote rehabilitation and successful reintegration.

Through these partnerships, detainees gain the tools and confidence to rebuild their lives, reconnect with their families, and contribute positively to their communities after release.

What We're Doing

Within the modified Community Empowerment Program (CEP), trained facilitators lead sessions in prisons that cover:

Human rights and civic responsibility.
Hygiene, health, and problem-solving.
Literacy and numeracy.
Preparation for reintegration and entrepreneurship.

Upon release, participants receive support to start small businesses and apply the knowledge gained during their training. Family mediation sessions, conducted before and after release, help restore trust and strengthen social reintegration.

Program Structure
Empowering Communities Through Partnership and Presence

When Tostan is invited into a community to begin the Community Empowerment Program (CEP), we assign a trained facilitator to the village. The facilitator is fluent in the local language and is often from the same ethnic group as the community members. Facilitators live in the village during the three-year program, getting to know community members. Tostan pays the facilitator and provides the curriculum, and community members house the facilitator and provide meeting space. These mutual commitments encourage everyone to be engaged with the program even if they cannot participate in classes.

Our program engages communities in two main ways: by providing human rights based education classes for adults and youth, and through the training and support of a Community Management Committee (CMC) designed to advance community projects.

Empowering Education

We see an important opportunity to invest in empowering education. Such an education prepares communities to better engage with the opportunities they have across education, health, economic empowerment, and many other issues. Nonformal empowering education fosters study and participation in activities that increase community well-being and can be very efficient in the longer term.

Classes

Each community runs two classes of 25 to 30 participants–one for adults and one for adolescents–that meet three times per week over the course of the program. By holding separate classes for the two groups, we ensure that both the youth and older community members can participate and contribute comfortably in the classroom while gaining the tools and confidence to actively apply what they learn in their community. Most participants have never been to formal school, or dropped out at an early age.

Tostan draws on modern nonformal education techniques as well as traditional African oral traditions like theater, storytelling, dance, artwork, song, and debate. By presenting information in ways that are relevant and engaging, we ensure the lessons resonate and new ideas take hold quickly.

The CEP classes have two phases: the Kobi, a Mandinka word meaning “to prepare the field for planting” and the Aawde, which means “to plant the seed” in Fulani.

About the Kobi

The Kobi, the first phase of the Community Empowerment Program (CEP), is structured to foster discussion and establish an open, inviting, and comfortable class dynamic. This helps participants feel more comfortable with the facilitator and each other. The goal of the Kobi is to promote positive traditions while encouraging discussion of how new ideas and practices can help build a healthier community. At the very beginning of this phase, community members establish a collective vision for their own development.

Signaler un abus

Tostan s’engage à garantir un environnement sûr, respectueux et digne pour toutes les personnes avec lesquelles elle travaille : membres des communautés partenaires, personnel, partenaires, prestataires et visiteurs.

Cette page vous permet de signaler tout comportement contraire à cet engagement. Chaque signalement est traité avec sérieux, confidentialité et diligence.

Notre engagement en matière de sauvegarde

La sauvegarde est au cœur de la mission de Tostan. Notre action repose sur la conviction que la dignité humaine est inviolable et que chaque personne, quel que soit son âge, son genre ou sa situation, a le droit d’être protégée contre toute forme d’exploitation, d’abus ou de violence.

Tostan a mis en place un ensemble de politiques pour traduire cet engagement en pratiques concrètes : une politique de prévention de l’exploitation et des abus sexuels, une politique de protection de l’enfant, ainsi qu’un code de conduite que signe toute personne associée à l’organisation, qu’elle soit membre du personnel, consultant, partenaire ou bénévole.

Ces politiques ne s’adressent pas seulement aux partenaires institutionnels ou aux équipes. Elles concernent en premier lieu les communautés avec lesquelles Tostan travaille au quotidien. C’est pourquoi l’ensemble de ces documents est disponible en pulaar, manding, bamananka, en créole portugais, en français et en anglais, couvrant les langues parlées dans nos zones d’intervention au Sénégal, en Guinée, au Mali, en Gambie et en Guinée-Bissau. Tostan considère qu’une politique de sauvegarde que les communautés ne peuvent pas lire dans leur propre langue n’est pas une politique de sauvegarde réelle.

Que peut-on signaler ?

Vous pouvez utiliser cette page pour signaler toute situation préoccupante, notamment l’exploitation ou les abus sexuels, le harcèlement sous toutes ses formes, la fraude ou la mauvaise utilisation des ressources, les abus de pouvoir, les représailles contre une personne ayant effectué un signalement, et tout comportement portant atteinte à la dignité ou à la sécurité d’une personne.

Cette liste n’est pas exhaustive. Si vous observez, subissez ou soupçonnez un comportement qui vous semble contraire aux valeurs de Tostan, vous avez le droit de le signaler.

Qui peut signaler ?

Toute personne en lien avec les activités de Tostan peut utiliser ce mécanisme : membres des communautés partenaires, personnel permanent ou contractuel, consultants, prestataires, partenaires, bénévoles, stagiaires, donateurs ou toute autre personne ayant été en contact avec l’organisation.

Confidentialité et protection

Tostan traite chaque signalement avec confidentialité. Les informations partagées ne sont accessibles qu’aux personnes habilitées à les examiner selon les procédures internes. Tostan s’engage à protéger contre toute représaille les personnes qui signalent de bonne foi.

Le signalement anonyme est possible. Si vous choisissez cette option, nous vous encourageons à fournir autant de détails que possible pour permettre un examen rigoureux de la situation.

Ce qui se passe après un signalement

Chaque signalement est examiné par les personnes compétentes selon les procédures internes de Tostan. Selon la nature et la gravité des faits rapportés, Tostan peut accuser réception lorsque des coordonnées sont disponibles, demander des informations complémentaires, mener une enquête interne, prendre les mesures disciplinaires appropriées, orienter la personne concernée vers un accompagnement adapté, et, si la loi l’exige ou si la gravité des faits le justifie, saisir les autorités judiciaires compétentes.

Tostan s’engage à agir avec objectivité, impartialité et rigueur dans le traitement de chaque cas.

Important

Cette page ne doit pas être utilisée pour des situations d’urgence mettant immédiatement en danger la vie ou la sécurité d’une personne. En cas de danger immédiat, contactez les autorités locales ou les services d’urgence de votre pays.

Pour toute demande générale concernant Tostan, utilisez les canaux de contact habituels de l’organisation.

Votre voix compte.

Signaler, c’est contribuer à un environnement plus sûr pour toutes et tous. Tostan vous remercie de votre confiance et s’engage à traiter votre démarche avec le respect qu’elle mérite.

Our Respect for Individual Privacy

Tostan’s work in every community is based on the simple premise of respect for each and every individual — and it’s also a premise we employ in our interactions with the global community, whether in person or online.

This page explains Tostan’s approach and commitment to respecting the privacy of our website users, what type of information we collect from our visitors, and how we use that information.

Information we collect about you and how we use it

We use Google Analytics on our website to track visitor traffic to the site. Google Analytics uses IP addresses to provide and protect the security of the service, and to give website owners a sense of where in the world their users come from. So when you visit the Tostan web site, we can determine the general location from which you are visiting. This information helps us diagnose any problems that may arise with our server and also gives us basic statistical information on visitor traffic. These IP addresses are not stored anywhere.

If you choose to sign up to receive Tostan’s monthly newsletter, you voluntarily provide us with your contact information (name, email, and organization). We use this information to provide you with email updates about Tostan, and to communicate with you should you have questions or requests for our office. You may choose to opt out of these communications at any time, at which point you will no longer receive any communication from us. Your contact information will still reside in our Salesforce database (the security of which is managed by Salesforce) should you ever wish to resume communication with our organization.

Email Privacy

Tostan does not provide, sell, or rent email addresses to anyone outside the organization.

Your Donation Information

Donating through Tostan’s website is a safe and simple process. We use a secure, well-known platform called Classy to process all donations that are made through Tostan.org. Classy collects your first and last name, mailing address, phone number, and email to send you receipts and manage your donation account. Your credit card information is collected and stored by Classy’s secure servers that are monitored 24/7 for security issues. This information is used to track and record transactions, and is not shared with any organizations other than Tostan. Tostan receives only your contact details and the amount of your donation. This information is tracked in Salesforce; we never have access to your credit card information. To read Classy’s privacy policy, please click here. If you have donated online since we transitioned to Classy in March 2018, you can manage your information preferences through their website here.

When you donate to Tostan via check, we collect your name and contact information and store it in Salesforce. We do not provide, sell, or rent your personal information to anyone outside the organization, nor do we send correspondence on behalf of another organization.

Cookies

We like to eat them, but we use them sparingly on our web site!
A cookie is a small script placed on the hard drive of your computer for the purpose of recognizing you when you return to our web site. The only cookies we use on Tostan.org are re lated to our use of Google Analytics. While these cookies do not provide us with any personal details about you, they help us understand how you use the Tostan web site—what links you click, what pages you access on a regular basis. This information helps us see what areas of our web site are most popular, and what areas of our site need to be improved. Tracking how you use our web site allows us to continue to improve your experience with Tostan.org.

If you prefer to keep your site usage private, Google has created a browser add-on that blocks sites from keeping track of your interactions. You can download and install this add-on here.

Links To Other Sites

We frequently share links to other sites and organizations that are in line with Tostan’s mission and vision. These sites all have their own privacy policies…so once you leave Tostan.org, we can’t be responsible for any privacy issues you may encounter on those sites.

What happens to my information if the site gets hacked?

We wish we could say that the information you provide us will never be compromised in any way, but we operate in a digital world where the threat of hacking and data theft is a common reality. Although we take steps to protect the safety of your data, including regular security updates and patches to our web site platform, we do not guarantee the security of your personal information transmitted through our website. If we discover that your personal information has been compromised, Tostan’s policy is to inform you immediately via email, provide regular updates on the situation until it is resolved, and provide you with any additional information or steps you can take to ensure the protection of your personal information. Tostan strives to address security threats, viruses, and hacking issues swiftly and immediately.

If you notice something unusual or suspicious on our web site, please email us at info@tostan.org to report it.

Changes to this policy

While our foundational premise of respect for your personal privacy will never change, it’s possible that the details of this document will need to be updated or amended from time to time. If we make any changes or updates, you’ll see a notice posted visibly on our web site. We’ll take your continued use of our web site, after posting notice of updates, as an indication of your agreement with any changes made to this document.

Questions or comments about Tostan’s privacy practices?

Feel free to email us here.

Tostan Addresses Menstrual Health Insecurity in Women’s Prisons
March 2, 2026
2 min read

The detention conditions of women reveal specific challenges that remain underaddressed, particularly regarding menstrual hygiene and health.

Thiès, March 2, 2026 – As the world prepares for International Women’s Rights Day, Tostan is implementing a targeted initiative across several prisons in Senegal to improve hygiene conditions for incarcerated women.

In 2024, Senegal held more than 14 147 detainees in facilities designed for fewer than 10,000 people, resulting in an occupancy rate of approximately 140%. This overcrowding weakens detention conditions and complicates access to healthcare, water, and sanitation services. Although women represent less than 3% of the prison population, they face specific needs that are still insufficiently addressed, particularly in terms of reproductive health and menstrual hygiene.

Official reports highlight gaps in medical follow-up and hygiene conditions, exposing incarcerated women to increased risks of infections, including gynecological conditions. Irregular access to sanitary products makes menstrual management especially difficult for women with low financial resources.

In response to these challenges, Tostan is distributing reusable hygiene kits in five women’s prisons, including Dakar, Thiès, Rufisque, Mbour, and Diourbel. These kits include washable sanitary pads and essential hygiene items. Food donations and financial support will also be provided to assist the most vulnerable detainees.

An Education Program in Prison Settings

“Women’s rights do not stop at prison gates. In detention, lack of access to hygiene can turn menstrual insecurity into a real risk to women’s health and dignity,” said Rose Diop, National Coordinator of Tostan Senegal.

This initiative is part of Tostan’s Prison Project, currently implemented in nine detention facilities across Senegal. The program provides human rights education sessions, vocational training, awareness activities, family mediation, and support for social reintegration.

In 2025, more than 1,700 women and girls have been supported both during detention and in their transition back into society.

About Tostan

Based in Senegal, Tostan operates in four West African countries and has supported communities for over 30 years in achieving their vision of well-being grounded in human rights. Through its community education program delivered in local languages, the organization strengthens governance, improves social conditions, and expands opportunities for women and youth.

More information: https://tostan.org/our-work/modules/prison-project/

Tostan CEP, The Classroom That Brought Me Back to Life
August 4, 2026
5 min read
Many young people never finish their education, not for lack of ability, but for lack of one thing: money, distance, or a family that needed them home instead. Edrisa Janko was one of them. 
He dropped out of school in Grade Nine after his father died, and spent five years watching his classmates move forward while he stayed behind.Then he joined Tostan’s Community Empowerment Program, first as a participant, later as a Community Facilitator, teaching neighbors about rights, dignity, and the power of education. But the lessons he delivered to others began working on him too. Every session he taught, he was also learning: that his circumstances did not have to determine his future.
That realization pushed him back to school after five years away. Scholarships and mentors carried him through secondary school, teacher training, and finally law school in Rwanda.On July 29, he took the oath as Barrister and Solicitor of the Supreme Court of The Gambia. Today, he serves as Tostan’s Human Resources Officer, using his legal training to protect staff rights in the organization that once believed in him.
This is his story, in his own words.

There are moments in life that quietly change everything. For me, that moment did not happen in a courtroom. It happened in a village classroom.

When I lost my father at the age of eleven, my world changed overnight. I was in Grade Seven, and my mother, who lives with a disability, struggled to keep our family afloat. We fought to keep me in school, but by Grade Nine, the burden had become too heavy. There was no money for fees, uniforms, or books. I dropped out.

For five years, I watched life move on while my dreams stood still

In my community, many believed that once a child dropped out of school, that chapter of life had ended. I tried to accept that reality. I worked, survived, and carried the silent pain of seeing my classmates continue their education while I remained behind. Deep inside, I still dreamed of returning to school, but I could not see a path.

Then Tostan entered my life

I first joined Tostan as a participant in its Community Empowerment Program. Later, I became a Community Facilitator. At the time, I thought I was simply helping communities learn. I never imagined that I was the one who would be transformed.

Every session challenged me to think differently. We spoke about human rights, dignity, equality, responsibilities, and the power of education. For the first time, I understood that education was not merely about earning certificates. It was about unlocking human potential, finding your voice, and believing that your circumstances do not have to determine your future.

Those lessons did more than educate me; they awakened me

Tostan planted a seed of hope that had long been buried beneath years of disappointment. It made me ask myself a question that changed my life:

“If I encourage others to believe in their future, why shouldn’t I believe in mine?”

That question became my turning point

I made the difficult decision to return to school after five long years away from the classroom. It was not easy. I was older than all of my classmates. I had forgotten much of what I had learned. I had no financial security. But I had something far more powerful than fear; I had purpose.

With determination, I resumed my education. Later, the Bansang Educational Appeal supported me throughout my senior secondary education. After graduating with excellent results, financial realities led me to pursue Higher Teachers’ Certificate at Gambia College instead of university.

Even then, my dream did not die

At another crucial moment, a remarkable man, Bram Kloos, believed in me and sponsored my university education. His generosity carried me through university and eventually to Rwanda, where I pursued my professional legal training.

Every stage of my journey was built upon people who believed that education could change a life

This month, I was formally enrolled as a Barrister and Solicitor of the Supreme Court of The Gambia, after my initial admission as Barrister and Solicitor at Supreme Court. Standing before the Court to take that oath was overwhelming. I remembered the frightened teenager who had believed his education had ended forever. I remembered the five years outside the classroom. I remembered every setback, every disappointment, and every person who refused to let me give up.

Today, I proudly serve as the Human Resources Officer at Tostan, the very organization that helped me rediscover my dream. My legal training now strengthens the work we do to protect labour rights, uphold fairness, and ensure accountability within the organization that first taught me the value of human dignity.

Looking back, I realize that Tostan did much more than teach me lessons. It restored my confidence. It gave me hope when I had almost none. It helped me understand that education is one of the greatest forms of empowerment because it changes not only what you know, but also what you believe is possible.

My story is proof that a classroom like Tostan CEP can change a destiny

To Tostan, thank you for seeing potential where others saw limitations. Thank you for teaching me that every human being deserves dignity, opportunity, and the chance to learn. Thank you for reminding me that education is not simply the path to employment; it is the path to freedom.

From a village classroom of Tostan’s CEP to the courtroom of the Supreme Court, this journey belongs to everyone who believed in me including Tostan.

And it all began with one lesson that changed my life, Tostan’s CEP.
May keep Tostan moving

Cheikh Anta Diop Fellowship Cohort 2 Opens- Apply Now
July 23, 2026
2 min read

Tostan has officially opened applications for the second cohort of the Cheikh Anta Diop Fellowship for Community-Led Development. The program targets young professionals and initiative leaders working across a wide range of community development fields—including health, education, the environment, governance, human rights, youth engagement, economic inclusion, and social cohesion.

These young leaders often have a solid grasp of their respective sectors. They possess expertise, drive, and ongoing projects. However, the ultimate success of their work relies on a critical, cross-cutting capability that is rarely taught: building trust-based relationships with communities and genuinely working alongside them.

The Cheikh Anta Diop Fellowship equips young leaders with a participatory educational approach that places communities at the heart of their own development. The program builds concrete skills to:

Establish trust rooted in active listening and mutual respect;
Understand local realities, aspirations, and existing community assets;
Facilitate inclusive dialogue where every voice is heard;
Co-design projects and solutions directly with the people affected;
Support communities without taking over or deciding for them.
Accompagner les communautés sans agir ni décider à leur place.

The program spans four months. It begins with an intensive 10-day residential seminar at the Tostan Training Center in Thiès, Senegal, followed by three months of mentoring, peer-to-peer learning, and individualized support.

Who Can Apply?

Young leaders aged 18 to 35 who are serving communities, active within an association, community initiative, NGO, social enterprise, civil society organization, public institution, or international organization, and available to complete the full four-month program, including the 10-day residential training, are eligible to apply.

Applications close on August 2, 2026.
