Community of Practice

for Amplifying Sustainable Community Well-being

The Community of Practice for Amplifying Sustainable Community Wellbeing is a dynamic, interactive platform that brings together development professionals who are committed to human rights and community-led approaches. It provides space to share experiences, learn from one another, and collectively advance skills, knowledge and understanding of community-led development.

By participating in the Community of Practice, you can:

Engage in meaningful discussions on various topics related to community development, human rights, and best practices.

Share your own experiences, challenges, and success stories with your peers, contributing to a wealth of knowledge and promoting continuous learning.

Connect with like-minded professionals from different organizations, sectors, and countries, expanding your network and opening doors to friendship, professional support and opportunities to collaborate.

Access state-of-the-art resources, tools, and case studies to inform and enhance your work–from Tostan, other members, and global leaders in community development.

Participate in webinars, workshops, and training sessions organized exclusively for the CoP members to further their professional development.

Who can join ?

Alumni of Tostan’s Training Center seminars are invited to join this diverse, passionate network of individuals dedicated to applying the
knowledge and skills gained during the training to make a lasting impact. The Tostan Training Center provides valuable training and
resources to organizations across Africa and beyond, supporting them with skills, methods and knowledge to drive positive change through
community-led development.

To support alumi’s ongoing learning and growth, the Community of Practice is a collaborative platform designed to facilitate knowledge
exchange, foster peer-to-peer connections, and enhance professional development.

Contact us if you have any questions or would like to say hello !

Join The COP
What to expect from the Community?
Continuous Learning and Growth

Join a supportive environment where you can build on your existing knowledge, explore new ideas, and refine your skills. By actively engaging with this vibrant community, you will stay abreast of the latest trends and developments in the field, ensuring your work remains relevant and impactful.

Peer-to-Peer Support
Connect with development professionals, activists, researchers and supporters from diverse backgrounds, fostering camaraderie and mutual support. By sharing your experiences and learning from others, you can overcome challenges, find inspiration, and gain valuable insights that can inform your own work for sustainable development.
Networking and Collaboration
Connect with peers from around the world, including alumni of the Tostan Training Center. The Community of Practice is a vibrant platform design for you to form lasting relationships and open doors to potential partnerships. It aims to provide opportunities to leverage collective expertise and resources of the community to amplify your impact.
Access to Exclusive Resources
You will have access to a wealth of resources, tools, and case studies designed to support your ongoing learning and professional development. These resources can help you deepen your understanding of community-led development and human rights, equipping you with the knowledge and skills needed to drive meaningful change in your community.
Recognition and Visibility
The Community of Practice is an opportunity to elevate your profile within the Tostan Training Center alumni network and the broader development community. By actively contributing to the community, you will showcase your expertise, demonstrate your commitment to continuous learning, and gain recognition for your work.
Community of Practice Governance
The Community formally launched in July 2023. It is co-created and co-led by a team of Tostan Training Center alumni known as the ‘Lafia Group’, hosted by Tostan serving as the Secretariat.

“We Were Taking It as Our Fight”: How Tostan’s Model Changed Our Approach in Ghana
July 21, 2026
4 min read

After completing Tostan’s training on the key principles and tools of its education model in Senegal, Philemon Puordeme Dong-Uuro, Head of Programmes at Vibrant Village Foundation Ghana, brought what he learned home. In this post, he shares how stepping down these core principles sparked an immediate paradigm shift and practical transformation within his team. “When you learn about an approach and tools so inspiring and humbling, you cannot wait to share the same with your colleagues,” he writes.

From March 17 to 19, 2026, VVF Ghana organized a three-day knowledge-sharing session for its staff on the principles, practices, and tools of Community-Led Development (CLD) inspired by Tostan’s well-being approach. This followed the participation of VVF Ghana’s Head of Programmes, Philemon, in a 10-day training session facilitated by Tostan in Senegal in February 2026. The Tostan training was organized under the Ghana Community-Led Development Collaborative to build the capacity of partner organizations in promoting CLD across Ghana.

The step-down sharing sessions, facilitated by Philemon, brought together 12 staff members. These sessions did not seek to replicate the full Tostan training, but rather to share key insights that would ignite systemic curiosity and a passion for adapting, improving, and deepening existing approaches to community engagement.

Participants discussed ways of promoting meaningful dialogue, aligning individual and communal values, navigating social norms, and applying human rights principles to community-led development. Through practical, participatory exercises, they explored community visioning, Psychological Reactance Theory, and the reinforcement of parental responsibility.

What were the immediate reactions ?

By the end of the sessions, staff members were excited and eager to implement what they had learned. Several participants expressed a deeper understanding of past challenges when working in communities and resolved to adopt these new approaches to work with communities.
 
In the words of one staff member:

Now I understand why we keep having a tough time fighting early and forced marriages, as well as the elopement of girls. These practices are underpinned by deeply rooted social values… we were treating it as our fight, which made some community members see us as the enemy. Instead, we need to facilitate a process that enables them to recognize the negative impacts of these practices and take up the fight themselves. Only then can we truly support them.

Beyond core methodologies, staff appreciated simple, transformative practices like circular seating arrangements and using dance to open sessions. As another staff member noted:

This training was engaging and refreshing. I realized that after everyone danced—including the facilitator—it became so much easier for us to open up and participate. The circular seating arrangement also fostered real interaction. I know this will work wonders in the communities—there will be no ‘back-benchers.

What are the results so far ?

Realizing that we can refine what we are doing well while embracing new ways of working has sparked tremendous curiosity across our team. Staff are eager to see how these approaches will unfold at the field level.

Small, steady steps are already being taken to integrate these practices into ongoing interventions. For instance, during an education program review meeting in April, the Program Officer introduced the circular seating arrangement—with remarkable results. Teachers participated far more actively than in previous engagements.

What is next for us ?

VVF Ghana prides itself on being a learning organization. We are excited to embrace new methods, learn, unlearn, and relearn. A pilot community has already been selected, and we remain fully committed to participating in future Collaborative events as we walk the Ghana CLD journey alongside like-minded partners.

Why 72 Million Young Africans Are Still Waiting for an Entry Point ?
August 13, 2026
3 min read

Around 72 million young Africans are NEET, not in employment, education, or training, according to the International Labour Organization. Two thirds are young women. On a continent where more than 60 percent of the population, about 864.9 million people, is under 25, that number defines the region’s future.

That gap keeps widening. Africa’s population is projected to more than double by 2050, reaching 2.5 billion. Every year, 8 million to 11 million young people enter the labor market while the formal economy creates roughly 3 million new paid jobs.

The cost of this gap does not stop with the young women and girls who carry it first. Economies lose the output of a generation not working or training. Communities lose the caregivers, teachers, and leaders that education would have produced. Progress toward gender equality slows each time a girl’s education ends early.

For young women and girls, that gap means unequal access to learning, leadership, and opportunity. Across the continent, young women have the capacity to advance climate action, expand economic opportunity, and drive digital innovation. They have projects. They have dreams. Too often, structural inequalities in education, technology, decent work, and public life hold them back before those projects begin.

Edrisa Janko was once part of that number, in The Gambia, until a Tostan literacy class sent him back to school and eventually to the Gambian bar this July. Fatimata Madina Baldé was part of it too, in Guinea Bissau, when an arranged marriage ended her schooling. A Tostan class in Pulaar gave her a way back that never required a classroom desk again. She now leads outreach across dozens of villages, without ever earning a diploma.

A generation this large is often called Africa’s greatest asset. Without a foothold in school or work, it can become its deepest challenge. Yet young people keep building anyway, starting small trades, organizing savings groups, teaching each other what schools did not. Governments that fail to open a formal path are not stopping that resilience. They are failing to match it.

Most of them left school early, or never enrolled, in places formal education never fully reached. For them, the way back rarely looks like a classroom desk. It looks like literacy and numeracy taught in their own language, tied to decisions they already need to make: pricing a harvest, keeping a savings group’s books, sitting on a village water committee.

Tostan has run that sequence for more than 35 years. Each community defines its vision first. Literacy and practical skills follow, built to serve that vision, not a standardized curriculum.

Yet the approach remains underfunded. National budgets favor formal schooling while non-formal education relies mostly on donor grants. Programs stall for lack of steady financing. African governments have pledged, under the UN Sustainable Development Goals, free secondary schooling for every child by 2030.

This week’s International Youth Day theme, Different Contexts, Common Aspirations, names exactly this reality. As UN Youth Envoy Jayathma Wickramanayake put it:

Young people are not the leaders of tomorrow, we are the leaders of today.

Seventy two million are still waiting for the door that would let them prove it. Funding non-formal education at scale is not charity. It is the fastest way to open that door, and it should start now.
